headlines.article_text: Rapidan Energy sees oil spike as U.S.-Iran military action risk rises Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Bob McNally, CEO of geopolitical and energy analysis firm Rapidan Energy Group said he foresees a 80% chance that the world will see "a resumption of military fighting." He predicts that both Brent and West Texas Intermediate futures will jump above $100. Iranian speaker of parliament Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has taken aim at U.S. Vice President JD Vance, calling his reaction to the Republican loss in the midterms a "losing gambler energy." A flight deck director signals an F-35C Lightning II on the flight deck aboard the USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) during Exercise RIMPAC (Rim of the Pacific) 2026 while underway in the Pacific Ocean near Hawaii on July 17, 2026. Michelle Bir | Afp | Getty Images The U.S. is likely to resume military action against Iran in the coming days, a move that could send oil prices sharply higher, according to Bob McNally, CEO of geopolitical and energy analysis firm Rapidan Energy Group. Speaking to CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ," McNally put the odds of "a resumption of military fighting" at 80% as the U.S. midterm elections recede. McNally said he expects both Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude futures to rise above $100 a barrel. The benchmarks are currently trading at about $100 and $91, respectively. watch now VIDEO 4:50 04:50 80% odds of renewed military attack in Iran, oil risk premium to head higher Squawk Box Asia Oil prices had spiked above the $100 mark ahead of the midterm elections as investors weighed uncertainty surrounding the Iran conflict and the risk of further U.S. military actions. President Donald Trump had previously said he would not launch new attacks on Iran before the elections, though The Wall Street Journal revealed that Washington had carried out limited strikes, according to U.S. officials. "President Donald Trump is determined, as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, having them give up their nuclear capabilities," McNally said. "The Iranian regime, on the other hand, is not willing to do it. And as long as that core difference in that deal space is absent, the escalation dynamic remains in place," he added. McNally's view is shared by other analysts, including Lombard Odier's chief economist Samy Chaar and head of investment strategy Luca Bindelli. In a Nov.4 note , they said the "lame duck" period before the new Congress is sworn in could give Trump a window to resume strikes against Iran. Any renewed campaign, however, could be constrained in duration and effectiveness by pressure on U.S. munitions supplies. Other analysts see the midterm results as creating more room for diplomacy. Norbert Rücker, head of economics and next generation research at Julius Baer said the market had become "more convinced" that the end of the midterms could provide a diplomatic off-ramp rather than lead to renewed escalation. That possibility increased with Iran reportedly sending the U.S. a nuclear proposal through Qatar, Reuters reported Friday, citing a senior Iranian official . But the proposal would be discussed only after Washington meets what Tehran described as "seven demands," ‌including an end to U.S. "acts of aggression," the naval blockade of Iranian ports and what it called economic warfare, as well as the release of Iranian assets. In return, Iran will allow ships to proceed freely through the Strait of Hormuz. The official also told Reuters that Washington was reviewing the proposal but ​declined to provide further details. Political fallout grows Separately, Iran's speaker of parliament Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf took aim at U.S. Vice President JD Vance after Vance blamed the war with Iran for Republicans' midterm losses. In a post on X , Ghalibaf described Vance's reaction as "losing gambler energy" and said that Vance "can't walk away from the table." He also accused the Trump administration of preparing the next phase of conflict. "Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?" Ghalibaf wrote, in an apparent reference to Trump. Iranian Parliament Speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, gestures while speaking with media in a media conference at a conference hall in the Iranian Parliament building in Tehran, Iran, on Dec. 2, 2025. Morteza Nikoubazl | Nurphoto | Getty Images Vance posted on Nov. 4 that "the reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," adding that a pollster he consulted found that ending the war was the top issue cited by former Trump voters who had switched to Democrats. Cost of living and inflation were also among these concerns. Vance has at times pushed for diplomacy with Tehran. The Wall Street Journal reported last week that he had reached out to an Iranian hard-liner in an effort to revive peace talks. The war has also contributed to higher global energy costs, which have fed into broader concerns over inflation and the cost of living. headlines.article_text: Tesla, SpaceX stocks fall after 2026 midterms Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX lose over $420 billion in combined market cap in the two days after midterms. As Democrats control the House and Senate, and Texas flips blue, investors expect Musk and his companies to face probes and steeper regulatory hurdles to their AI and merger ambitions. Musk was the biggest backer of GOP candidates and causes in the midterms and most of those he backed were defeated by Dem opponents. In this article TSLA SPCX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT SpaceX CEO Elon Musk looks on as President Donald Trump speaks to the press after a meeting with technology executives about artificial intelligence at the White House in Washington, Sept. 29, 2026. Kent Nishimura | AFP | Getty Images SpaceX and Tesla shares declined by about 9% and 11%, respectively, on Thursday afternoon with investors concerned that Elon Musk could face new congressional probes — and his companies stricter regulation — following the U.S. midterm elections. The declines, which correlated with a broader tech sell-off , brought aggregate market cap losses for SpaceX and Tesla to over $420 billion since Tuesday's close. Musk's wealth, which had topped $1 trillion after SpaceX's initial public offering in June, is now down below $800 billion, having dropped about $90 billion in the past week, according to Forbes . He is still the richest man in the world. Musk was the biggest donor to GOP candidates and causes in the midterms, with his financial contributions exceeding $470 million , the Financial Times first reported. Despite his bolstering the GOP war chest, most of the candidates Musk backed lost their races . Democrats won control of both the House and Senate. And in Texas, where both Tesla and SpaceX are headquartered, Democrats Sen.-elect James Talarico and Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa beat longtime Musk allies, state Attorney General Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott. Deutsche Bank analysts wrote in a note out on Wednesday, "While policy is naturally hard to predict, we could envision SpaceX facing some incremental headwinds in this type of backdrop." Gov.-elect Hinojosa "made data centers a major campaign issue," the analysts noted, calling for "a moratorium on new approvals until the legislature passes stronger protections on water use, electricity costs, local control, and incentives," and criticizing tax breaks for large facilities. Tesla and SpaceX are both building out AI infrastructure in Texas, and are planning to build Terafab, a massive facility, which will include a data center and sprawling semiconductor factory, in Grimes County, Texas. SpaceX also plans to build out a "supercomputer" at its Starbase, Texas, launch facility and company town, according to company job listings . Deutsche Bank analysts also wrote that SpaceX's Texas compute capacity could now be at risk of delays. Capital expenditures by the company may need to increase to meet the requirements of tighter, anticipated regulations around data center buildout, the analysts wrote. Musk and SpaceX have been instructed to preserve records concerning restrictions imposed on a military version of the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, CNN first reported , citing an aide to a Democratic senator. The restrictions hampered the country's ability to defend against attacks by Russia. Additionally, regulatory scrutiny could block chances for Musk to merge SpaceX and Tesla, an idea he has promoted, while acknowledging shareholders' approval would be required first. SpaceX and Tesla had lost about $456 billion in market cap by the close of business on Thursday. -- CNBC's Nick Wells contributed reporting. I-Hwa Cheng | Bloomberg | Getty Images Asian technology stocks tumbled Friday, tracking a sharp sell-off on Wall Street overnight that sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite into correction territory as renewed concerns over artificial intelligence spending rattled investor sentiment. South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix plunged over 8%, while Samsung Electronics shed 7%. LG Innotek and LG Display fell 10% and 7.7%, respectively, as selling pressure spread across the country's technology sector. In Japan, semiconductor-related stocks also fell, with chip-testing equipment maker Advantest plunging 12.2%, while Tokyo Electron slid 7.3%. Technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 11.6%. China was also caught in the regional sell-off, with the tech-heavy STAR Market and the ChiNext Artificial Intelligence Index both tumbling more than 4%. The declines followed a brutal session on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite sank 5.5%, amid mounting concerns over the sustainability of the AI investment boom and returns on massive data-center spending.
